title: Good Influence at Scale
subtitle: Help others succeed beyond your immediate team
summary: Influence at scale comes from relationships, teaching, writing, and structures that let good decisions travel. Staff engineers build bridges across teams, form coalitions, and adapt a message to stakeholders rather than relying on authority they do not possess.

concepts.title: Influence
concepts.body: Influence changes decisions through trust, evidence, and relationships when formal authority is absent. Advice works better when you understand what the other person is trying to accomplish and whether they want advice. Ask before prescribing. Trust and relevant context make a recommendation usable; seniority alone does not make it the right answer.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A support report and a design note persuade through evidence rather than rank.

concepts.title: Stakeholders
concepts.body: Stakeholders experience different consequences and hold information needed for a workable decision. Listen for the constraints behind a position rather than treating disagreement as ignorance. Different teams may have legitimate goals that the proposed change affects differently. Understanding those needs helps you find an intervention that people can actually sustain.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: Support, product, and engineering name different consequences of the same outage.

concepts.title: Teaching
concepts.body: Teaching scales judgment by giving groups models, examples, and practice they can apply independently. Repeated individual advice can become a shared guide, workshop, or other teaching opportunity. Choose a format that lets people practice and ask questions. The purpose is to help them apply judgment later, rather than requiring your presence for each repeat problem.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A brown-bag session lets teams practice the new review technique.

concepts.title: Bridge
concepts.body: A bridge translates between teams or disciplines while preserving the important meaning on both sides. Connect people who have complementary knowledge, and translate the context each side is missing. Often the highest-value contribution is enabling a conversation or removing an obstacle. A catalyst helps useful work happen without needing to own its eventual credit.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: The staff engineer translates customer language into a decision the owning team can act on.

misconceptions.claim: a staff-plus role is mainly about applying a universal formula.
misconceptions.correction: The chapter treats judgment as contextual: identify forces, listen to evidence, and adapt the response to the actual system and people.

misconceptions.claim: A visible activity or artifact proves the work is complete.
misconceptions.correction: Completion requires a useful outcome, shared understanding, and a way to notice whether the decision worked over time.

scenario.title: Build influence
scenario.context: Support reports recurring customer pain, but the owning team distrusts architecture proposals. You have no authority to mandate a redesign.

options.label: Listen and bridge
options.benefit: Clarifies the decision and creates a workable path through the stated constraint.
options.cost: Listening may reveal that the proposed technical fix is not the customer’s highest-cost problem.
options.consequence: You collect support examples, invite the team into the diagnosis, and co-author a small experiment.

options.label: Publish a mandate
options.benefit: Feels faster or safer in the immediate moment and preserves a familiar habit.
options.cost: A mandate spends relationship capital and invites quiet resistance.
options.consequence: The proposal may be technically sound, but the team lacks ownership and quietly routes around it.

scenario.debrief: Both options respond to a real constraint. The stronger choice makes ownership and consequences visible, then creates a point to learn and adjust.

quiz.question: Before giving unsolicited advice, what is a useful first step?
options: Ask what the person needs and whether advice would help
Explain why their approach is wrong
quiz.explanation: Understanding the need and obtaining an opening makes advice more useful.

quiz.question: The same question repeatedly reaches you from different teams. What may scale your help?
options: A shared teaching session with practice and examples
Requiring your approval for the task
quiz.explanation: Teaching can help many people apply the idea independently.

quiz.question: What does acting as a catalyst emphasize?
options: Receiving visible credit for every improvement
Connecting people or removing obstacles so useful work can happen
quiz.explanation: Influence can enable an outcome without retaining ownership of it.

exercise.title: Make the next move legible
exercise.prompt: Describe a staff-level decision, the people and terrain involved, and the route by which you will learn whether it worked.
